**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The cursor blinks, a silent metronome counting down the seconds until I must begin. A thousand words—how heavy they feel when the mind is a blank slate, how light when the heart is full. I wonder if words are like feathers or stones, depending on who holds them.

I think of the first time I understood the power of language. I was seven, sitting cross-legged on a classroom floor, listening to my teacher read *Charlotte’s Web*. When Wilbur was spared, I cried—not because a pig lived, but because words had made me care. That was the first time I realized stories could reach inside you and twist something loose.

Now, years later, I sit with my own blank page, my own silent audience. What do I owe them? Truth? Beauty? A distraction from the weight of their own lives? Maybe all I can offer is this: a confession that I don’t know what I’m doing, that every sentence is a step into the dark, and yet I keep walking.

Outside my window, the world moves in its usual chaos. A dog barks. A car honks. Somewhere, a child laughs, and for a moment, the sound is enough to make me forget the weight of the words I’m supposed to write. But then the silence returns, and the cursor blinks again.

I remember reading that Hemingway once said, “There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed.” But what if you don’t have a wound to open? What if all you have is the dull ache of ordinary days, the quiet accumulation of moments that don’t quite add up to meaning?

Perhaps that’s the real work—to find the sacred in the mundane. The way light slants through a window at 3 p.m. The way coffee tastes better when it’s raining. The way a stranger’s smile can feel like a lifeline.

I think of all the words I’ve ever read, the ones that stayed with me. They weren’t always the grandest or the cleverest. Sometimes they were just the right ones at the right time. A line from a poem. A sentence in a letter. A whispered “I understand” when I thought no one did.

Words are bridges. They are lifelines. They are the things we throw into the dark, hoping someone on the other side will catch them.

And so, with 800 words left, I keep writing. Not because I have something profound to say, but because the act itself is a kind of faith. A belief that if I keep going, something true might emerge. That if I string enough words together, they might form a rope strong enough to pull me—and maybe someone else—out of the silence.

The cursor blinks. The page is no longer blank. And for now, that’s enough.
